Russia's own figures show almost 500,000 deaths in war in Ukraine
articles.summary: Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked
articles.body: At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC. The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old. BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow. Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked. Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records. The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict. The data also reveal the extent of losses in specific areas of Ukraine. Some 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of 10 Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000. During the fight for one small village called Andriivka, south of the town of Bakhmut in Donetsk region, 1,122 Russians lost their lives. Before the war 74 people lived there. Russia does not give public figures for losses sustained since the war began in February 2022. And two years ago Rosstat stopped publishing data of deaths from external causes, which was used to gauge the extent of military losses. For example, only 70% of deaths we have established of soldiers from the occupied regions of Donetsk and Luhansk in eastern Ukraine who fought in the Russian army were accounted for in the Rosstat files. The Rosstat dataset contains no names but does include ages, places of residence, places of death and also circumstances of death. We have filtered the records first by location, leaving only Ukraine as well as Russian border regions that saw incursions by the Ukrainian army. Next, we identified 425,174 entries explicitly indicating a military-related cause of death, such as explosions or shrapnel during combat operations. As this count could include civilians, we filtered out women as well as men outside the 18-65 age group. And if someone lived and died in the four Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, we excluded them as a possible civilian – unless he had a record of military service attached to his entry. Another 14,093 entries were identified by looking at employment, and 51,067 were recorded in the database as deceased on the basis of a court ruling. This often happens when a soldier goes missing in a combat zone for more than six months and their body has not been recovered. Again, we filtered out civilians by only counting deaths in the war zones in Ukraine and Russia. BBC Russian's own detailed records of Russian losses has reached 290,012, verified together with Mediazona from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves. The actual death toll is likely to be higher, as not all deaths are reported publicly. Overall, the Rosstat dataset confirms the trends that we have observed with our own count. According to BBC Russian's analysis of the leaked files, in the first year of the war the average age of those killed was 34. By 2025, as prisoners and contract soldiers entered the ranks, it had risen to 40 (38 according to our own list). Some of Russia's poorest regions in Eastern Siberia account for a disproportionately large share of the losses. Men from Tyva, Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai are 20-25 times more likely to die in the war than residents of the biggest cities of Moscow and St Petersburg. In most regions, the distribution of deaths based on Rosstat data differs from that in the BBC's list by just a few tenths of a percentage point. At least 5,017 foreigners are among those who died fighting for Russia, according to our analysis of the Rosstat files, including 1,031 Uzbeks and 720 Tajiks. We have left out Ukrainians from this count to avoid including civilians. This is a conservative estimate as dual nationals are listed as Russians in the database, and there is no reference to North Koreans who died repelling the Ukrainian incursion into Russia in 2024. The BBC identified 2,304 North Korean soldiers who died there by analysing satellite imagery and official photographs of a newly built memorial in Pyongyang. The leaked Russian statistics may not be complete but taken in conjunction with BBC Russian's own work they are significant. Military experts estimate that the BBC's figure of 290,012, gleaned from open sources, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll – ranging from 527,295 to 644,471. In the context of a war that has lasted four years and 10 months, these are high numbers for Russia, when compared with the Soviet war in Afghanistan that ended in 1989. Ukrainian losses were last put at about 50,000 by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July 2026, but another list based on open sources by the anonymous UA Losses website puts the figure at 115,952. articles.title: Qatar condemns ‘shameful’ Houthi attack on Riyadh tower
articles.body:
Qatar has strongly condemned the Houthi attack on a tower in the financial centre of Saudi Arabia’s capital Riyadh, calling it “a shameful act of aggression, an unacceptable disregard for civilian lives, a flagrant violation of Saudi sovereignty, and a clear breach of the rules of international law”.

The ministry also reaffirmed Qatar’s full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and its support for all legitimate measures that the kingdom takes to preserve its sovereignty, security, territorial integrity, and interests.

It added that Saudi Arabia’s security is an integral part of Qatar’s security and the collective security framework of Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) member states.

articles.title: Iran orders Hormuz closed 'further day by day' as Qatar seeks to revive peace talks
articles.summary: The IRGC claimed three tankers hit mines in the crucial strait while under US escort
articles.body: Iran's army commander-in-chief ordered his navy on Monday to close the Strait of Hormuz "further day by day" until Washington meets Tehran's conditions, warning that any new US military action would draw blows that were "more severe, more crushing and without geographical limitation.""Until the seven conditions of the Islamic Republic of Iran are fulfilled, not only will the Strait of Hormuz not be opened, it must be closed further day by day, conditions for the enemy must become more difficult, and stronger control will be exercised over it," Major General Amir Hatami said, addressing senior commanders of Iran's armed forces.Citing orders from Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, Hatami added that if the US "commits a new folly and starts another war, in the new phase the blows will be more severe, more crushing and without geographical limitation."The elite paramilitary IRGC said on Monday that three oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz suffered "powerful explosions and massive fires" after hitting naval mines.One tanker was hit off the southern shores and two more in the east of the strait, "while under extensive air escort by the US army," an IRGC statement said.The IRGC said it would publish images of the explosions and warned shipowners that "military escort by the US army is no substitute for compliance with maritime regulations."The Joint Maritime Information Centre (JMIC), in a report covering 19 to 21 November, said it recorded 114 passages through the strait "with the assistance of the United States" and that claims of tankers hitting naval mines were unconfirmed.Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Washington was seeking to impose a neither-war-nor-peace situation on Tehran, threatening there were "military ways to break the blockade that, God willing, we will pursue in the near future."As head of the Iranian delegation in the Islamabad talks, Ghalibaf said there would be no further negotiations or action before Washington moved."Before the implementation of Iran's seven conditions there will be no action and no negotiation, and in response to the enemy's moves we are also ready to give a decisive answer and to change the geography of the battlefield in the event of an enemy mistake," Ghalibaf said.Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told reporters a naval blockade was "tantamount to military aggression" and that Iran had "the right in this regard to use any available means to defend itself.""We will certainly not tolerate this situation, and we will use all our tools to confront this US aggression," he said.Qatar wants both sides at the tableQatar's Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani visited Washington on Monday and met US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President JD Vance to discuss efforts to restart negotiations between Tehran and Washington.After his talks with Rubio, Al Thani said the region "cannot bear a renewed escalation of tensions between the United States and Iran" and that Doha was working to bring both sides back to the table.Qatar and the US were also seeking to strengthen their military cooperation, he said. According to AP, citing a source familiar with the proceedings, the meeting with Vance lasted about 10 minutes.The visit followed US President Donald Trump's statement on Sunday that military strikes on Iran could resume after the New Year. Trump had said earlier this month that he had asked Vance to shift his focus from Iran to domestic policy.In recent days, Iran has attacked US military bases in Bahrain and Kuwait on several occasions, and Tehran's armed forces have reported almost daily that tankers it describes as violators have struck naval mines.Qatar hosts the largest US military base in the Middle East and the regional headquarters of CENTCOM, and plays a key mediation role between Tehran and Washington.

articles.summary: The decision establishing it was approved by the legal committee on rules and immunities
articles.body: Subcommittee for parliamentary oversight of implementation of decisions of European Court of Human Rights and judgments of Constitutional Court set up The Subcommittee for parliamentary oversight of the implementation of decisions of the European Court of Human Rights and judgments of the Constitutional Court has been established. The decision establishing it was approved by the legal committee on rules and immunities. The Subcommittee will have three members: MPs Pavel Voicu, who was also designated as chair, Vasile Grădinaru and Igor Chiriac. In its work, the Subcommittee will permanently monitor the process of implementing the decisions of the European Court of Human Rights, as well as the judgments of the Constitutional Court. It will also promote the draft legislative acts necessary for their implementation. The Subcommittee will also hear the authorities responsible for developing and implementing the measures necessary to execute the judgments and decisions of the European Court of Human Rights and the judgments of the Constitutional Court, and may request information from those authorities. According to the Regulations of Parliament, the chair of the Subcommittee will annually present a report to a plenary session of Parliament on the implementation of the decisions of the European Court of Human Rights. articles.title: The Constitutional Court's review of "Georgian Dream's" lawsuit to ban five opposition parties has been postponed until November 30
articles.summary: This information was confirmed to InterpressNews by the Constitutional Court
articles.body: The Constitutional Court's review of "Georgian Dream's" lawsuit regarding the banning of five opposition parties has been postponed until November 30. This information was confirmed to InterpressNews by the Constitutional Court. According to them, the next hearing will be held on November 30 at 12:00. According to available reports, the reason for postponing the hearings was the death of the father of one of the judges. For reference, the review of the lawsuit in the Constitutional Court began on October 21. The case is being examined by a seven-judge plenum of the Constitutional Court. The lawsuit submitted to the Constitutional Court is signed by 88 members of Parliament. Based on their lawsuit, the issue of declaring the following five political associations unconstitutional is on the court's agenda: "Unity – National Movement"; "Coalition for Change – Gvaramia, Melia, Girchi, Droa"; "Strong Georgia – Lelo, For the People, For Freedom!"; the "Federalist Party"; and the party "Gakharia for Georgia." The constitutional lawsuit is accompanied by the conclusion of the temporary investigative commission established in the 11th convocation of Parliament.

articles.title: Grigol Gegelia: I am glad that Kulevi will not be used as part of Russia's war economy - this is good, and once again I regret that Georgia has a liar for a Prime Minister
articles.summary: I would like to welcome the news that the Kulevi oil terminal will no longer be on the sanctions list
articles.body: "I am glad that Kulevi will not be used as part of Russia's war economy - this is good, and once again I regret that Georgia has a liar for a Prime Minister," - this is how Grigol Gegelia, Foreign Secretary of Strong Georgia - Lelo, responded to media reports that the European Commission is proposing to European Union member states to remove the Kulevi oil refinery from the sanctions list. According to Grigol Gegelia, we are witnessing "yet another shameful lie" from the Prime Minister "when he claims that there were supposedly no grounds whatsoever for the potential sanctioning of this terminal." "I would like to welcome the news that the Kulevi oil terminal will no longer be on the sanctions list. This is good for our country. I wish the oil terminal success for the benefit of Georgian national interests and the interests of the Georgian economy. At the same time, we are witnessing yet another shameful lie from Irakli Kobakhidze when he says that there were supposedly no grounds whatsoever for the potential sanctioning of this terminal. I would like to remind him of the statement made by the leaders and executives of this very terminal on April 1, when they said that yes, problems existed, and requested a six-month period until autumn in order to fix these problems and come into compliance with international standards. Apparently, they fulfilled this and succeeded, and that is precisely why today the European Union is announcing that the Kulevi oil terminal will not be included in international sanctions—not because there were no grounds for concern previously. Once again, I am glad that Kulevi will not be used as part of Russia's war economy—this is good, and once again I regret that Georgia has a liar for a Prime Minister," Grigol Gegelia notes. As a reminder, the European Commission has submitted a proposal to European Union member states to remove the Kulevi oil refinery from the sanctions list. The outlet writes that amid the threat of sanctions from the European Union, the Kulevi oil refinery decided to diversify its oil supply sources by replacing Russia. It should also be noted that on July 23, the Council of the European Union adopted the 21st package of EU sanctions against Russia, which included the Kulevi oil refinery. Within the framework of the sanctions, the European Union adopted a transaction ban against the refinery and set its entry into force for 6 months.

articles.title: Minister on new constitutional provision: Interior ministry proposed idea of stripping of Armenia citizenship, it has 2 layers November 24, 13:12
articles.summary: We still have to open a field for discussion around the idea
articles.body: During the discussions of the draft constitution, the Ministry of Internal Affairs itself submitted that proposal, and I am glad that the final publicized version contains that regulation. The Minister of Internal Affairs of Armenia, Arpine Sargsyan, on Tuesday told this to reporters, referring to the fact that the draft of the new constitution of Armenia contains a provision according to which in the case of crimes against the constitutional order and national security, a person can be stripped of Armenian citizenship by a court. “We still have to open a field for discussion around the idea. But various countries have the institution of revoking citizenship for this group of crimes, because in these conditions, the person, one might say, is so dangerous that states raise the question of whether they should continue to have contact with the given person, whether or not to define the scope of rights or obligations inherent to a citizen. But there are various layers here, the same situation in the logic of applying it to dual citizens, the same situation in the logic of applying it to persons with citizenship of only one country. I think we will still have time to discuss [it] in order to understand the regulations,” Sargsyan said. But the minister added that by including the aforesaid provision, they do not mean anyone in particular. “The issue is ideological, because our current constitution does not give the possibility of revoking [Armenian] citizenship. If we [i.e. Armenia] now provide for the institution of revoking in the law on citizenship, it will be unconstitutional. This is the reason why we propose to provide for such an opportunity in the text of the constitution, so that later we can make amendments to the law on citizenship and provide for the procedure. We accept that there are two layers: dual citizens’ part and citizens who have only the citizenship of the Republic of Armenia. Along with this, we also have an international obligation that states must do everything so that there will be no stateless persons, as such, at the global level. We naturally acknowledge, understand all these layers. We also have international practice on our side in this regard, we will move forward with discussions, we will understand what the final settlement will be like. But don't worry, nothing will be envisaged that is unconstitutional or does not comply with our international obligations,” Arpine Sargsyan said. She noted that even today there are people in Armenia who do not have citizenship or are considered refugees. “This does not mean that they cannot live or use various services in the Republic of Armenia,” the interior minister added. The draft of the new constitution of Armenia, which was publicized on Monday, proposes to eliminate the ban on stripping of Armenian citizenship. According to the draft, a person can be revoked of Armenian citizenship only by court decision and in cases provided for by law; for example, on the basis of committing crimes against the foundations of the constitutional order or national security of Armenia.

articles.title: SDA: Constitutional Court of BiH Ruling confirms that the Lilies and Symbols of the Army of the RBiH cannot be banned
articles.summary: The ‘lilies’ and the symbols of the ARBiH are part of the historical and state heritage of BiH
articles.body: The Party of Democratic Action (SDA) welcomes the decision of the Constitutional Court of BiH, which ruled that a provision in the Criminal Code of the Republika Srpska (RS) entity—prohibiting and criminalizing the display of flags and symbols of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina—is unconstitutional. According to an SDA statement, this decision confirms the position the party has consistently and unequivocally maintained from the outset: that banning the symbols of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina (ARBiH) violates the Constitution of BiH and its constitutional-legal continuity, and that no entity has the right to challenge the symbols of the legitimate army of an internationally recognized state. The request for a constitutional review—submitted by 11 members of the House of Representatives of the Parliamentary Assembly of BiH—was drafted by SDA legal experts, giving concrete form to the previously announced legal battle against attempts to ban the symbols of the ARBiH. “The ‘lilies’ and the symbols of the ARBiH are part of the historical and state heritage of BiH. It was under these symbols that the independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of our state were defended. The ARBiH was the sole legitimate armed force of the internationally recognized Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and its legacy and insignia are recognized today even within the Armed Forces of BiH. Attempts by the authorities of the Republika Srpska entity to rewrite historical facts by criminalizing these symbols—thereby equating the defenders of BiH with the forces responsible for the aggression and the gravest war crimes—constitute an unacceptable assault on the truth and the legal order,” the SDA statement reads. The SDA will, it is added, continue to use all available legal and political mechanisms to protect the constitutional order of BiH, its historical heritage, and the dignity of the state’s defenders.

articles.summary: This gives them a lot of ammunition
articles.body: Fox News host Jesse Watters said Monday that President Trump’s defense of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang will give Democrats “ammunition” to go after the president — and potentially pursue impeachment. “The Democrats are now licking their chops over the Jensen affair and Trump personally restoring him as CEO, even if it was to help the economy and the country,” Watters said. “This gives them a lot of ammunition. The Democrats will likely use this scandal to impeach.” Huang was restored as CEO on Monday despite revelations of extramarital affairs — including one with a woman the U.S. government suspected of being a Chinese spy — after Trump’s public and private defense of the tech executive. Trump said he personally urged the board to restore Huang to lead the company he co-founded, and a source confirmed to The Hill that Vice President Vance also played a role in the push. Huang’s return to Nvidia drew bipartisan scrutiny and is likely to be the subject of congressional investigations. The CEO is already set to testify before the Senate Banking Committee, and Republicans are even calling for Congress to investigate Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, the suspected spy. With Democrats set to reclaim majorities in both chambers next year, investigations are even more likely to take place. Democrats are "going to say Trump put our national security at risk and is bowing to the Chinese, and a bunch of Republicans in Congress aren't going to defend him, so this is going to get ugly — fast,” the “Primetime” host said. “And a billionaire, foreign-born chip king, a Republican donor, who cheats on his wife and is tech war profiteering, isn't the most sympathetic character for the president's party to defend,” he added. Top Democrats have not said they plan to impeach Trump, but they have not ruled it out either. In a recent interview with The New York Times, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said he has faith in Democrats to properly seek accountability. “I have great trust in the legislative leaders of this effort and every single Democrat who’s on the Oversight Committee. We’ve done accountability in this Congress,” Jeffries told the Times. Democrats impeached Trump twice in his first term, and he was acquitted on both occasions. Several Democrats have expressed concern that moving to impeach him a third time could backfire, and it would be unlikely to yield a conviction even with Democrats’ expanded Senate majority.

articles.summary: Another man, Djordje Zdrale, currently on the run, is suspected of the attempted murder
articles.body: Naser Oric, a former commander of Bosniak forces in Srebrenica during the 1992-5 war in Bosnia, was arrested on Tuesday as part of an investigation into an attempted in East Sarajevo in August. Jelena Miovcic, from the State Investigation and Protection Agency, SIPA, confirmed that Oric was arrested in the Olovo area in the country’s Federation entity. Miovcic also confirmed that Nikolina Sljivic, a former member of the national assembly in Bosnia’s Republika Srpska entity, had also been arrested, adding that police are investigating the attempted murder of the man, named as Kosta Pandurovic, in East Sarajevo. Another man, Djordje Zdrale, currently on the run, is suspected of the attempted murder. In another, related development, the Republika Srpska Interior Ministry, MUP RS, said it was carrying out an operation codenamed “Emisar” targeting an organised criminal group, with five people arrested so far. “Searches are being conducted at several locations across Republika Srpska and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including properties owned by Djordje Zdrale, who is being actively sought by MUP RS,” the ministry said. Bosnia’s top court, the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, previously sentenced Zdrale to 20 years in prison for the murder of Ljubisa Savic Mauzer, former head of the Republika Srpska Police Administration, in June 2000. He was released from prison in February 2022 after the Court of consolidated his sentences and determined he had served the combined sentence. Oric earlier faced trial for war crimes but was acquitted. In 2008, the Appeals Chamber of the UN International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, ICTY, acquitted Oric of failing to prevent the murder and cruel treatment of Serb prisoners. This ruling overturned a first-instance conviction. In 2018, the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina acquitted him of murdering three Serb prisoners in the Bratunac and Srebrenica areas during the war in Bosnia.

Houthi media says 25 killed or missing after Saudi strikes
articles.body:
Houthi-affiliated news agency Saba said Tuesday that a Saudi strike on buses and trucks had left 25 people dead or missing in Yemen's southwest.

The Iran-backed fighters, who control swathes of Yemen, are battling a Saudi-led coalition that supports Yemen's internationally recognised government.

"The toll from the Saudi enemy planes' targeting of buses and trucks in Wadi Mabaq, Lahj Governorate, has risen to 25 martyrs or missing, and six wounded," reported the Houthi-run Saba news agency, adding that the continued presence of Saudi aircraft over the area was hindering rescue efforts.

On Monday, the Houthi's military spokesperson Yahya Saree had reported the attack — without providing casualty figures — and vowed it would not go "unanswered."

Separate strikes on Monday killed 17 people and destroyed several buildings in the neighbouring coast province of Hodeida, the Houthis' telecommunications ministry said.

articles.body:
President Trump said Tuesday that the United States is taking more oil through the Strait of Hormuz than it did before the war with Iran.

"We're taking more oil through the Hormuz Strait right now than we did before the war started, and oil is, as you just heard, coming down to very reasonable numbers," Mr. Trump told reporters ahead of the annual Turkey pardon. "People, it's dropping very quickly, like a rock."

The price of Brent crude has dropped to its lowest level since late August.

The president also said the U.S. military has not allowed any Iranian ship to get through the naval blockade since it was established, with the exception of the brief moratorium over the summer.

"Iran is in the process of developing chemical weapons," Katz said in a briefing to Israeli reporters, according to public broadcaster KAN and other national outlets. "The state of Israel will not allow them to reach that capability."

In his briefing on Tuesday, Katz floated the possibility of a preemptive strike against Tehran, if necessary.

"If we recognize that the Iranians intend to attack Israel, can't we tell the army to attack earlier and thwart the threat?" he said, according to a transcript from Israel's Channel 12. "If the Iranians attack us first, it will be a failure."

Katz's comments came at the same time as Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi criticized the U.S. government for not funding the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, the international body that monitors and combats chemical weapons use at The Hague. The organization is facing a budget crisis because the U.S. has pulled funding, according to a Reuters report.

"The U.S. is so concerned about chemical arms that it's crippling the world's chemical weapons watchdog," Araghchi wrote Tuesday on X. "OPCW may be forced to suspend work and scale back vital programs. By obstructing its mandate, the U.S. is deliberately putting global peace and security at risk. Shameful."

The OPCW won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2013 for its work in Syria.

CBS/AFP

editorialRejections.body: BUDAPEST, November 25. /TASS/. The Hungarian government has agreed to open the final two chapters of negotiations on Ukraine’s accession to the European Union, but the process will follow the standard rather than an accelerated procedure, Prime Minister Peter Magyar said at a press conference following his meeting with Vladimir Zelensky in the city of Beregovo. "Hungary, together with the other 27 EU members, has agreed to send letters concerning the fourth and fifth negotiating clusters, which have yet to be opened," Magyar said. He recalled that, under the established procedure, "this will be followed by an intergovernmental conference at which a formal decision will be made" to launch negotiations on the two remaining groups of issues. At the same time, he emphasized that "accession to the European Union must be based on an assessment of actual achievements, and this is an incredibly difficult path." "There is simply no such thing as an 'accelerated procedure,' and the European side does not recognize it. Let me be clear, and I hope you understand me correctly: there is no ‘fast-track procedure,’" Magyar said. Last summer, Hungary’s new government withdrew its objections to the launch of EU accession talks with Ukraine and Moldova. This came after the Ukrainian authorities pledged to restore the rights of the Hungarian ethnic minority in Transcarpathia. Budapest and Kiev reached an agreement on the matter, which became part of Ukraine’s EU accession plan. Nevertheless, Magyar has repeatedly warned that Hungary opposes Ukraine’s accelerated admission to the European Union and that the country must meet the same requirements as other candidates. He has also noted that negotiations with Ukraine could be suspended if it fails to fulfill its commitments to Hungary. editorialRejections.title: NATO allies anxious as war spreads beyond Ukraine, Russia borders As Ukraine attacks Russian ships in far-flung waters, some NATO nations are voicing increasing anxiety over the war's spread to new regions.
editorialRejections.summary: We assume this was an intentional act
editorialRejections.reason: Routine, incomplete or malformed headline outside the DNU brief
editorialRejections.body: Some NATO countries are voicing increasing anxiety as hostilities in the nearly five-year war sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine spread beyond the two countries' borders.Polish authorities accused Russia again Tuesday of deliberately violating the nation's airspace as officials said a surveillance drone briefly crossed the Polish border before turning back into Ukraine. Poland, a member of the U.S.-led NATO alliance and a neighbor and close ally of Ukraine, accused Moscow of a deliberate provocation late last week after three Russian missiles landed on Polish soil.Polish Deputy Defense Minister Paweł Zalewski said in a radio interview on Tuesday that the Russian drone crossed the border for a "very short time" and was "monitored from the very beginning.""I spoke with the Operational Command of the Armed Forces, and the decision was made not to shoot it down, as they did not want to risk any casualties or damage on the civilian side," Zalewski told Radio Poland. "We assume this was an intentional act."A "need for stability in our near areas"Norway's Defense Minister Tore Sandvik said Tuesday, meanwhile, that the Scandinavian country was speaking with Ukrainian officials about the "need for stability in our near areas," following a strike on Saturday that hit a U.S.-sanctioned Russian cargo ship in international waters in the Gulf of Finland.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy acknowledged Ukraine had carried out that strike in a social media post on Monday, saying the country's forces used seven domestically produced naval drones to attack the ship.The Sparta II cargo vessel, which is operated by Russian defense logistics firm Oboronlogistika, has been under U.S. sanctions since 2022 for illicit transportation of military hardware. Russian authorities confirmed that it had been towed back to a Russian port on Tuesday.Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani spoke Tuesday with his Ukrainian counterpart Andriy Sybiha, meanwhile, in a phone call to express Italy's concern over another Ukrainian attack carried out over the weekend, this one off the coast of Libya.Zelenskyy lauded Ukrainian forces on Monday for that attack, which sank a Russian warship and damaged another U.S.-sanctioned Russian cargo vessel, the MV Angara, off the North African nation's Mediterranean coast, where Russia has a naval base."The minister emphasized to his Ukrainian counterpart how crucial it is for Italy to keep working to prevent the conflict with Russia from spreading into the Mediterranean," Italy's Foreign Ministry said Tuesday in a readout of the ministers' call.Zelenskyy framed the strikes on the Russian ships as legitimate defensive actions in response to Russia's ongoing deadly missile and drone strikes, which it launches from land, sea and air."Despite all the enemy's efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk," Zelenskyy said. "We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia's aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons."The Russian Foreign Ministry this week accused Estonia, another NATO ally, of being "on the verge of triggering open war" after the small Baltic country announced it would close its land border with Russia starting Dec. 1.Estonia accused Russian intelligence agencies last week of a plot to infiltrate and sabotage the domestic defense company Threod Systems."Any attempt to threaten Estonia's security, sow fear, or act hostilely against us will be met with a decisive response," Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said in a statement last week. "By closing the border crossings, we are sending a clear message to the Kremlin: Russia's hostile actions come at a cost. The more aggressively Russia behaves, the narrower its room for manoeuvre becomes."The Estonian move came only a couple of weeks after Poland's prime minister said a large-scale security operation launched along the Polish-Russian border may have prevented a sabotage or provocation operation by Russian operatives."Ukraine is doing exactly what they need to do"While NATO members' concern over the spread of the war has been more clearly iterated in recent weeks, Ben Hodges, a former top commander of the U.S. Army in Europe, told CBS News on Tuesday that, in his opinion, all of Ukraine's actions constitute a legitimate defense in the face of Russia's aggression."Ukraine is doing exactly what they need to do to disrupt Russian oil/gas exports and other international activities to degrade Russia's ability to sustain its war effort," Hodges said. "This is also an important signal to anyone who would willingly support Russia's shadow fleet."Moscow uses its so-called shadow fleet — hundreds of dubiously registered tankers — to evade international sanctions on its oil sales, keeping money flowing in to power its war machine.Hodges told CBS News that Kyiv has likely calculated the risks involved in attacking Russian vessels in neutral waters."The risk is that Russia will attempt to use these as an excuse for its attacks against the Ukrainian economy and civilian infrastructure," he told CBS News. "But Ukraine knows this and anticipates it.""Most European countries also already understand this and will not be moved by it," he added.

editorialRejections.title: November 24, 2026 - 17:40 Russia's war against Ukraine could reach turning point in 2027, Latvian president says

editorialRejections.body: Russia's war against Ukraine could reach a turning point in the spring or summer of 2027, driven by Russia's deteriorating economy and mounting international pressure on Moscow, Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs said in an interview with Reuters.When the war could reach a tipping point Rinkēvičs believes the war could reach a tipping point next year that would eventually lead to Moscow's defeat. However, he linked such a development to Ukraine's ability to withstand military and economic pressures. If we see Ukraine surviving from a military point of view, from an economic point of view - and I'm sure Ukraine is going to survive - then the tipping point could be next year, next spring, next summer, the Latvian president said. According to him, Ukraine is facing a perfect storm: a harsh winter, intensified attacks on energy infrastructure, and strikes on civilian facilities. However, Ukraine has repeatedly demonstrated its resilience, and Europe is ready to support it with military, financial, and infrastructure assistance. Pressure on Russia will increase In addition to Russia's deteriorating economic situation, Rinkēvičs pointed to a growing international consensus on the need to end the war. As an example, he cited attacks that killed Indian sailors or hit vessels from the Philippines and other countries. In his view, this demonstrates that the consequences of the war are extending beyond the immediate conflict zone. The number of countries that are putting pressure is going up so the tipping point ​may come in spring, summer, next year, Rinkēvičs emphasized. At the same time, the Latvian president does not believe Moscow is genuinely interested in ending the war. In his view, the Kremlin likely sees renewed ceasefire negotiations as a distraction allowing it to continue its invasion. Russia is becoming more willing to take risks Rinkēvičs also expressed concern over an increase in hybrid activities against European countries that are likely linked to Moscow. These include airspace violations, cyberattacks, and acts of sabotage. In his assessment, Russia is still carefully avoiding crossing the threshold that could trigger NATO's Article 5 on collective defense. However, Moscow's willingness to take risks is growing. The Latvian president noted that European intelligence services are improving coordination and intelligence sharing, making it possible to prevent attacks in some cases. Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs previously warned of Europe's vulnerability to Russian missile attacks. According to him, NATO countries are failing to keep pace with advances in aerial warfare technology, while Moscow is using sabotage and cyberattacks to test their resolve to support Ukraine. Amid negotiations aimed at ending the war, discussions on security guarantees for Kyiv continue. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy previously highlighted the uncertainty surrounding security guarantees modeled on NATO's Article 5 and later described Ukraine's accession to NATO as a simpler solution, as there is still no clear answer as to who would defend the country and how in the event of another Russian attack.

editorialRejections.title: What would constitutional change unlock for North Macedonia?
editorialRejections.summary: North Macedonia is being asked to amend its Constitution to enumerate Bulgarians among the communities listed in its Preamble
editorialRejections.reason: What explainer headlines are excluded
editorialRejections.body: North Macedonia is being asked to amend its Constitution to enumerate Bulgarians among the communities listed in its Preamble. The change is presented as the step that would allow EU accession negotiations to advance. Yet the government opposes proceeding without safeguards against further Bulgarian conditions. The change may appear modest: the 2021 census recorded 3,504 residents identifying as Bulgarian. Why should explicitly naming this community in the Constitution create such a problem? The answer lies in Bulgaria’s position on Macedonian identity itself. In its 2020 Explanatory Memorandum, circulated to EU member states , Bulgaria portrays Macedonian identity and language as artificial creations imposed by Yugoslav communism to erase the population’s alleged Bulgarian identity. The underlying logic closely resembles Putin’s denial of Ukraine’s distinct nationhood : the neighboring nation is claimed as part of one’s own, and its distinct national identity is treated as a product of communist engineering. The issue therefore extends far beyond the status of a small community. Constitutional inclusion would give Sofia an additional basis for presenting demands over Macedonian history and identity as protection of that community. The existing accession arrangements already allow Bulgaria to invoke bilateral commitments to withhold consent to progress. This article examines how that pressure could operate through disputes over census results, historical teaching and commemoration, and communist-era archives. The route into accession was to present Bulgaria’s detailed demands as implementation of the 2017 Treaty of Friendship between Macedonia and Bulgaria , even where they extended substantially beyond its express provisions. The Treaty established general commitments to cooperation. Article 12 created a joint intergovernmental commission to review implementation and agree measures. In October 2019, Bulgaria adopted its Framework Position , setting out its conditions for supporting Macedonia’s EU progress. These included demands concerning historical teaching, archives, public inscriptions, alleged hate speech, and state-funded cultural production. In November 2020, Bulgaria blocked approval of the EU negotiating framework . The French EU presidency brokered arrangements to overcome that blockade in July 2022. Macedonia accepted the Second Protocol , a bilateral document adopted through the Treaty’s intergovernmental commission under Article 12. The Protocol turned many of Bulgaria’s demands into detailed commitments presented as implementation of the Treaty . The EU negotiating framework then made Treaty implementation, expressly including these Article 12 reviews and measures, part of the assessment of accession progress . The Council of the EU’s conclusions also expressly welcome the Protocol. The European Commission’s 2026 report already treats implementation of the Protocol as essential. It also records that the separate historical commission established under the Treaty met four times “but without tangible outcomes.” The Treaty established that commission; the Protocol subsequently specified expectations of clear results and their implementation in education. The Commission’s assessment thus already reflects the Protocol’s emphasis on historical results, even before the constitutional amendments. At accession decisions requiring unanimous consent, Sofia can invoke these commitments to justify withholding approval. Bulgaria already describes them as European obligations and constitutional inclusion as only the first step . Its demands thus return as European commitments North Macedonia is expected to fulfill. The following three situations draw on Bulgaria’s existing positions and conduct to show what demands it is likely to pursue during negotiations after constitutional inclusion. Consider Bulgaria’s challenge to the 2021 census , which recorded 3,504 residents identifying as Bulgarian. Sofia invokes much larger figures: in July 2024, President Rumen Radev said that at least 120,000 Macedonian citizens had obtained Bulgarian citizenship through documented Bulgarian origin. Deputy Foreign Minister Marin Raykov claimed in April 2026 that more than 210,000 people from North Macedonia had documented Bulgarian origin. Setting these totals against each other makes the census appear to have missed a large population, although citizenship records cannot establish how many residents identify as Bulgarian. Vasiliki Neofotistos documented Macedonians seeking Bulgarian passports for mobility and economic opportunities, while Mina Hristova’s fieldwork recorded people maintaining Macedonian identification while acquiring Bulgarian documents. Their accounts show why a declaration made to obtain citizenship cannot simply replace the identity people express in their own country’s census. Ancestry documents do not settle the question either. An ancestor’s administrative or religious classification requires interpretation and does not automatically establish their national self-identification, still less a descendant’s. Citizenship records establish what applicants declared and Bulgarian authorities accepted as grounds for granting citizenship; they do not determine those applicants’ ethnic identification as citizens of North Macedonia. Bulgaria’s policy nevertheless collapses those distinctions. Its 2014 national strategy counts Macedonian citizens who acquired Bulgarian citizenship after 1990 among ethnic Bulgarians. Its Foreign Ministry questioned the census while invoking citizenship figures, applying a revealing double standard: the declaration that brings an EU passport is taken at face value, while the one that brings no such benefit requires an explanation. The Protocol’s provisions on Bulgarian rights give Sofia a way to bring this population claim into accession negotiations. They require “sustainable results” in protecting Bulgarian identity without specifying how those results are to be measured, and conspicuously cite neither the Framework Convention for the Protection of National Minorities nor the European Convention on Human Rights. Bulgaria’s April 2026 statement on the minority-rights Action Plan already connects discrimination allegations to its conditions for supporting accession progress. Sofia could portray the gap between the existing census results and its population claims as evidence of continuing suppression and a hostile anti-Bulgarian climate, echoing accusations already advanced in its 2020 Explanatory Memorandum . Its own population claims would then become the test of the census’s credibility. On that basis, it could maintain a blockade and demand a new census or special verification, insisting on assurances that the results would reflect its claims about the number of Bulgarians. The practical problem is therefore who decides what counts as adequate protection. European standards protect freely expressed identity. Bulgaria’s approach allows the failure to declare the identity Sofia expects to become evidence that this identity is being suppressed. The same claim of suppressed Bulgarian identity extends into historical teaching. Accepting Bulgaria’s account would mean teaching Macedonians that their present identity was constructed by suppressing an underlying Bulgarian one, with the implied prospect of “rediscovering” their alleged Bulgarian origins. The historical commission’s mandate is to discuss historical and educational questions, but discussion does not guarantee agreement. Experts can examine the same sources and disagree. The Protocol calls for intensified work and clear results . It also commits both governments to supporting and encouraging the commission to complete its work on “all periods” of what it calls common history, with the resulting recommendations fully implemented in education before North Macedonia joins the EU . Bulgaria’s Framework Position prescribes the conclusions: Macedonian history before 1944, when the Macedonian republic was established within Yugoslavia, is to be treated as Bulgarian history. Bulgarian co-chair Angel Dimitrov has defended the Memorandum as reflecting the achievements of Bulgarian historical scholarship. Yet a collective declaration by Bulgarian historians and other scholars rejected its underlying thinking as outdated, romantic, and mythological and opposed imposing Bulgaria’s official historical account. Dimitrov attributes his Macedonian colleagues’ resistance to political considerations , yet defending conclusions prescribed by his own government apparently qualifies as independent scholarship. The consequences of judging the commission by its results were already visible in the 2020 veto. In November that year, Foreign Minister Ekaterina Zaharieva cited insufficient progress in its work , and Bulgaria refused to approve the negotiating framework , citing inadequate implementation of the Treaty. Failure to agree on historical interpretations was thus treated as Macedonia’s failure to fulfill a bilateral obligation. The same reasoning could govern subsequent accession decisions: Sofia could make consent to the next stage conditional on a commission recommendation accepting its interpretation. Macedonian historians could attend every meeting, examine the evidence, and explain their disagreement, yet their work would count as insufficient. The demand would concern the conclusion they must reach, rather than whether the commission had done its work. Sofia could pursue historical revisions through minority-protection claims even without the commission’s agreement. The revolutionary Goce Delchev illustrates the stakes: Bulgaria claims him as Bulgarian and rejects accounts placing him within a distinct Macedonian national history. The commission has reached no agreement on him since its establishment in 2018. Although the Protocol provides for implementing agreed recommendations, Sofia could argue that such accounts deprive the constitutionally enumerated Bulgarian community of its heritage. It could then demand textbook changes and withhold accession consent on that basis. What Macedonian children learn about him would become a test of respect for Bulgarian rights. The same argument could extend across curricula, museums, commemorations, and other historical figures. The Protocol itself expressly includes textbooks and monument inscriptions in its procedures for identifying and addressing hate speech . Sofia could invoke those provisions to demand changes to accounts of Bulgarian wartime conduct, presenting such changes as protection of the Bulgarian community from alleged hostility. Bulgaria, an Axis ally of Nazi Germany , occupied much of what is today North Macedonia during World War II. Its authorities pursued coercive assimilation and violently suppressed resistance . As documented by the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum , Bulgarian military and police officials rounded up Jews and deported them into German custody. The International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance commemorates 7,144 Macedonian Jews deported to Treblinka. Objections to depicting this history have already been linked to accession. In 2011, Bulgarian MEPs accused the Macedonian film The Third Half of spreading hatred over its portrayal of wartime persecution; in 2012, Foreign Minister Nikolai Mladenov connected the controversy to Macedonia’s EU aspirations . The 2019 Framework Position subsequently demanded changes to inscriptions using formulations such as “Bulgarian fascist occupier.” Documenting the actions of state and occupation authorities does not assign collective guilt to Bulgarians today. Treating historical accountability as an ethnic insult shifts the accusation from those who committed the acts to those who document them. By contrast, portraying Macedonian identity as a falsification stigmatizes the national community and justifies pressure to change how it understands and presents its own history. The reversal is stark: denying Macedonian identity becomes a defense of historical truth, while documenting the Bulgarian state’s wartime conduct becomes hatred toward Bulgarians. The Protocol gives these accusations practical force through diplomatic monitoring and procedures for removal , while cultural funding can be suspended or recovered for breaches of hate-speech undertakings. Sofia could demand a changed textbook, a removed inscription, or a withdrawn exhibition, invoking these commitments to block accession progress. A dispute over historical presentation would become a demand to demonstrate compliance with European obligations against hatred. Yet those procedures cite no Council of Europe instrument and supply no criteria for distinguishing an account of state responsibility from hostility toward Bulgarians as a community. The Council of Europe’s approach requires proportionate responses that protect freedom of expression. The procedure does not explain how such accusations are to be tested against those standards, leaving room for Sofia to turn an allegation of hatred into a demand for removal and block accession progress until that demand is met. The Protocol extends this pressure into the communist-era archives, requiring a legal framework for opening state-security archives for 1945–1991 . It also requires reaffirming condemnation and an apology for what it calls “injustices and repressions committed in the past” by Yugoslav communist authorities based on “ethno-political self-determination,” including against Bulgarians. editorialRejections.title: Is Russia planning to launch a nuclear weapon into space? NATO chief responds
editorialRejections.reason: Question headlines are excluded
editorialRejections.body:
Yesterday, reports emerged in German news outlets that Russia may be planning to launch a satellite armed with a ⁠nuclear weapon ⁠into ​space.

According to broadcasters NDR and WDR, and newspaper Sueddeutsche Zeitung, the German intelligence service and armed forces have discussed a Russian satellite which they believe could be launched within 60 days.

Kremlin spokesperson ​Dmitry Peskov has rubbished the claims, saying "there are so many 'alleged' ​and 'possible' claims in it, attributed to who knows whom, that ⁠it's certainly hardly worth ​taking ​them seriously".

Asked about reports, NATO chief Mark Rutte said on Monday the alliance is constantly assessing its deterrence and defence situation.

"I can assure you, we will always make sure that we defend every inch of NATO territory. And that includes making sure that we are safe when it comes to the space element," he said.

Rutte said NATO has a variety of response options, even if the general public does not always see them.

Germany's defence minister urged people to stay coolheaded.

Boris Pistorius said: "First of all, let's remain calm."

"There ⁠are reports - ⁠that's true - but it's not ‌clear what kind of weapons these are, ‌and the effect they might have depends, in turn, on ⁠where they are deployed," he added.

"Therefore, ​it's too early to ⁠speculate publicly about this. We are ⁠consulting internally and ​taking the necessary ​measures."

While it sounds like something out of science fiction, sending such weapons into space would breach the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, of which Moscow is a signatory, as well as the 1963 Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty.

editorialRejections.summary: It was established by a decision approved by the Committee on Legal Affairs, Appointments and Immunities, IPN reports
editorialRejections.body: A parliamentary subcommittee will monitor how the authorities implement the judgments and decisions of the European Court of Human Rights, as well as the rulings of the Constitutional Court. It was established by a decision approved by the Committee on Legal Affairs, Appointments and Immunities, IPN reports. The subcommittee will consist of three members: Party of Socialists MP Pavel Voicu, who has also been appointed its chair, and Party of Action and Solidarity MPs Vasile Gradinaru and Igor Chiriac. The new body will continuously monitor the implementation of the rulings issued by the two courts and advance the draft legislation needed to give effect to them. The subcommittee will also be able to hear testimony from representatives of the authorities responsible for developing and implementing the necessary measures, and to request information on the actions taken. Under Parliament’s Rules of Procedure, the chair of the subcommittee will present an annual report to Parliament in plenary session on the implementation of the judgments and decisions of the European Court of Human Rights.

editorialRejections.body:
Two Libyan soldiers have died from injuries sustained in an attack, claimed by Ukraine, on Russian ships near Benghazi, a senior figure in the administration in eastern Libya said late on Tuesday.

Libya is divided between a UN-recognized government in Tripoli and a parallel administration in the east of the country, backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar.

Haftar's camp has maintained close military and strategic ties with Russia for several years.

His son Saddam Haftar, who is widely seen as heir apparent, said "it is with deep sadness and great pride that I pay tribute today to two heroes of our naval forces," following the attack.

They "were martyred as a result of their injuries sustained during the performance of their national duty following the criminal attack on the Benghazi Naval Base", he added on Facebook.
